leads.text: JWE decompression bomb (zip bomb) in jose/jwe.py: attacker-controlled `jwe_str` (parameter of the EntryPoint method `decrypt`, jose/jwe.py:60) flows through `_jwe_compact_deserialize(jwe_str)` (line 79, which unpacks attacker-controlled `header`, `cipher_text`, `iv`, `auth_tag`) into `_decrypt_and_auth(...)` (line 178), and the resulting `plain_text` is passed to `_decompress(header.get("zip"), plain_text)` at line 187, which reaches `zlib.decompress(compressed)` at jose/jwe.py:453 with NO `max_length`/size cap and no post-decompression length check. The attacker also controls the `zip` header value selecting the DEF (deflate) branch (line 452 `zip == ZIPS.DEF`). Critically, the authentication at line 240 is not a barrier for public-key JWE algorithms (RSA-OAEP / RSA1_5 / ECDH-ES are in ALGORITHMS.SUPPORTED): any attacker who knows the recipient's PUBLIC key can legitimately produce a correctly-authenticated JWE containing a highly-compressed payload, so the tag check passes and decompression proceeds. A ~50KB token can expand to multiple GB, causing unbounded memory allocation and denial of service.

leads.text: JWS/JWT algorithm-confusion via an INCOMPLETE HMAC-secret blocklist, enabling signature forgery. Attacker-controlled `alg` is read from the untrusted token header at jose/jws.py:250 (`alg = header.get("alg")`) and flows unsanitized into key construction: jose/jws.py:257 `_get_keys(key)` -> jose/jws.py:208 `jwk.construct(key, alg)` -> jose/jwk.py:76-79 `key_class = get_key(algorithm); key_class(key_data, algorithm)` -> jose/backends/native.py:23 `HMACKey.__init__(key, algorithm)`. An attacker who knows that public key can then mint a token with `alg: HS256` and a valid HMAC, forging arbitrary authenticated claims.

leads.text: Non-constant-time comparison of the attacker-supplied JWE authentication tag in jose/jwe.py:240 (`if auth_tag != auth_tag_check: raise JWEError("Invalid JWE Auth Tag")`), inside `_decrypt_and_auth`. The `auth_tag` operand is attacker-controlled: it is parsed from the untrusted token at jose/jwe.py:79 (`auth_tag = tmp0[5]` from `_jwe_compact_deserialize(jwe_str)`) and passed into `_decrypt_and_auth` at line 178 (FLOWS_TO arg_index 6), while `auth_tag_check` is the locally computed HMAC from line 232 `_auth_tag(cipher_text, iv, aad, mac_key, key_len)`. Python's `!=` on bytes is a short-circuiting byte-wise comparison, so its execution time is proportional to the length of the matching prefix, leaking the correct tag one byte at a time to an attacker who can time many decrypt attempts - permitting forgery of the AES-CBC-HMAC-SHA2 authentication tag. This is demonstrably an oversight rather than an accepted risk: the same codebase uses the constant-time primitive `hmac.compare_digest(sig, self.sign(msg))` at jose/backends/native.py:69 for JWS signatures. Additionally, line 239 performs `encryption_key.decrypt(cipher_text, iv, aad, auth_tag)` BEFORE the tag comparison at line 240, i.e. decrypt-then-verify ordering on the HMAC_AUTH_TAG path.

leads.text: MISSING MAC-BEFORE-DECRYPT ORDERING in JWE AES-CBC-HMAC: in `_decrypt_and_auth` (jose/jwe.py), the ciphertext is decrypted AND PKCS7-unpadded at line 239 (`plaintext = encryption_key.decrypt(cipher_text, iv, aad, auth_tag)`) and only AFTERWARDS is the HMAC authentication tag compared, at line 240 (`auth_tag != auth_tag_check`). For the `A*CBC-HS*` enc values the callee is CryptographyAESKey.decrypt (jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py:490), whose non-GCM branch runs `decryptor.update/finalize` (lines 507-508) and then `PKCS7(...).unpadder().update(padded_plain_text)` (lines 509-510) with no MAC check of its own. A PKCS7 unpadding failure therefore raises a different error than the `JWEError("Invalid JWE Auth Tag")` raised at line 241, giving an attacker a padding oracle (Vaudenay/Lucky-13 class) against attacker-submitted JWE tokens. The required control -- verify the HMAC tag over (aad||iv||ciphertext||al) BEFORE performing any CBC decryption or unpadding -- is absent.

leads.text: MISSING AUDIENCE ENFORCEMENT when the `aud` claim is absent: `_validate_aud` (jose/jwt.py:316) begins with the test `"aud" not in claims` at line 336, and the graph contains NO call nodes at all between line 336 and line 341 -- i.e. that branch performs an unconditional early return with no `raise`, even when the caller explicitly supplied an expected `audience`. The next executed statement is line 341 `audience_claims = claims["aud"]`. Combined with `require_aud` defaulting to False (jose/jwt.py:114), a token that simply omits `aud` is accepted by an application that passes `audience="my-api"`, so a token minted for a different relying party (same issuer/key) is accepted -- cross-audience token replay. The enforcement for the present-`aud` case does exist (line 348 `audience not in audience_claims` -> line 349 `raise JWTClaimsError("Invalid audience")`), which is what makes the absent-`aud` gap an asymmetric hole.

leads.text: NO `crit` HEADER PROCESSING ANYWHERE in the library: RFC 7515 s4.1.11 requires that a recipient REJECT a JWS/JWE whose protected header carries a `crit` member naming extensions the implementation does not understand. A repo-wide search for the string 'crit' across every CpgCall.code in the scan returned zero rows, so neither jose/jws.py's `_verify_signature`/`_load` nor jose/jwe.py's `_jwe_compact_deserialize` inspects it. `_jwe_compact_deserialize` only validates that the header is a JSON Mapping (jose/jwe.py:304-305) and `decrypt` only checks `alg`/`enc` membership (jose/jwe.py:92-98), so a token marking a security-relevant extension as critical is silently accepted and the extension ignored -- defeating any downstream security semantics the sender attached to it.

leads.text: CHECK NEUTRALISED INTO A TAUTOLOGY: in the AES-GCM branch of jose/jwe.py:_decrypt_and_auth, line 235 assigns `auth_tag_check = auth_tag` -- the attacker-supplied tag is copied into the variable it is about to be compared against. The explicit authentication-tag verification at line 240 (`if auth_tag != auth_tag_check: raise JWEError("Invalid JWE Auth Tag")`) is therefore dead code for every ALGORITHMS.GCM encryption: the condition can never be true. The explicit tag check that exists for the CBC-HMAC branch is thus structurally disabled for GCM, leaving tag integrity entirely dependent on the backend raising internally (cryptography_backend.py:503). A verifier should check whether every registered AESKey backend's decrypt() actually raises on a bad GCM tag -- if any backend returns plaintext instead, line 240 provides no backstop.

leads.text: Declared dependency `cryptography==39.0.1` is an outdated, known-vulnerable third-party component and is the primary crypto backend for this library (jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py imports Cipher/aead/algorithms/modes from it at line 10 and uses it for all RSA/EC/AES/HMAC operations). The exact-pin `==39.0.1` prevents any patch uptake. Publicly known issues fixed only in later releases include the Bleichenbacher timing oracle in RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decryption (fixed 42.0.0), NULL-pointer dereference on PKCS7 loading (fixed 41.0.6), and NULL-pointer dereference on malformed PKCS12 (fixed 42.0.2), plus the OpenSSL versions bundled in the 39.x wheels. Because this is the dependency that performs the actual RSA1_5 unwrap in this repo, the PKCS#1 v1.5 decryption oracle is directly relevant to the JWE decrypt path rather than theoretical.

leads.text: Declared dependency `ecdsa` uses the version specifier LITERAL `!= 0.15`, an exclusion with no lower bound, so dependency resolution may install arbitrarily old and known-vulnerable releases (e.g. 0.13.x, affected by CVE-2019-14853 malformed-signature DoS and CVE-2019-14859 signature-malleability). This pin shape is the defect: it blacklists exactly one bad version instead of requiring a minimum safe one. The pure-Python `ecdsa` library is used for real EC signature verification in this repo (jose/backends/ecdsa_backend.py maps NIST256p/NIST384p/NIST521p curves and constructs ecdsa.ellipticcurve.Point / ecdsa.SigningKey / ecdsa.VerifyingKey), and it additionally carries CVE-2024-23342 (Minerva timing side-channel on ECDSA nonce handling) for which upstream ships no fix, so ES256/ES384/ES512 signing here is side-channel exposed regardless of the resolved version.

leads.text: RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 key transport is enabled by algorithm-set LITERALS, exposing a Bleichenbacher / Million-Message-Attack padding oracle on the JWE decrypt path. jose/constants.py line 32 defines `RSA1_5 = "RSA1_5"`, line 54 puts it in `RSA_KW = {RSA1_5, RSA_OAEP, RSA_OAEP_256}`, line 55 folds that into `RSA = RSA_DS.union(RSA_KW)`, and line 70 unions RSA_KW into the `SUPPORTED` set used for validation -- so an attacker-chosen `alg: "RSA1_5"` in a JWE header is accepted. jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py line 223 binds it to the raw padding primitive `RSA1_5 = padding.PKCS1v15()` and line 238 wires it into the live dispatch dict `{ALGORITHMS.RSA1_5: self.RSA1_5, ...}.get(algorithm)` (reachable from entry). RSA1_5 unwrap has been deprecated precisely because distinguishable padding-failure behaviour yields a decryption oracle for the content encryption key; keeping it in the supported literal set means a caller cannot opt out via the JWE API.

leads.text: Several declared dependencies carry no lower-bound version constraint at all -- the version LITERAL is the empty string for `pyasn1`, `pycryptodome`, and `rsa`. leads.text: SHA-1 is hardcoded as a LITERAL choice in the RSA-OAEP padding construction: jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py line 224 reads `RSA_OAEP = padding.OAEP(padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA1()), hashes.SHA1(), None)`, using SHA-1 for both the MGF1 mask-generation function and the label hash, with no way for a caller to substitute a stronger digest. The adjacent RSA_OAEP_256 variant exists, so an application that negotiates plain `RSA-OAEP` silently gets SHA-1. Note this specific pairing is what RFC 7518 prescribes for the `RSA-OAEP` identifier, so it is spec-conformant rather than an implementation slip, and OAEP's security proof does not depend on collision resistance -- hence low severity. Flagging it only as a deprecated-primitive hardcoded literal worth confirming against the project's crypto policy; a verifier should not treat this as exploitable on its own.
